recognition.difference: The Riemann Hypothesis follows once $\zeta$ has no zero with real part above $1/2$: by the functional equation, the zeros in the critical strip are symmetric about the critical line. The book states the symmetry of the zeros and states the Riemann Hypothesis; it does not write this implication down as a separate result, it is immediate from the symmetry. The library takes its hypothesis for every Dirichlet character and uses it for the character of modulus 1 only. Its conclusion is the Riemann Hypothesis as Mathlib defines it, which is about zeros of $\zeta$ other than the trivial zeros $-2, -4, \dots$ and other than the point $1$, and the proof works with Mathlib's functional equation for $\zeta$ itself, not with $\xi$; it treats every $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s < 1/2$ at once, the trivial zeros showing up as zeros of the cosine factor, where the book's symmetry is stated for the zeros of $\xi$.
recognition.result: the symmetry of the zeros of $\zeta$ about the critical line, from the functional equation

conditions: At modulus 1 the only character is the trivial one; it counts as primitive and its $L$-function is $\zeta$. The half-plane then contains $s = 1$, where $\zeta$ has its pole and Lean gives $\zeta(1)$ the defined value $(\gamma - \log 4\pi)/2$, which is not $0$; so at that one point the statement asks for a nonzero value of a convention, not about a zero.
claim.text: for every primitive Dirichlet character $\chi$, of any modulus $N \ge 1$, $L(\chi, s) \ne 0$ whenever $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$

citations.source: H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I (Cambridge University Press, 2006), Chapter 10
citations.where: Section 10.1, p. 333 ("The conjecture that these latter zeros all lie on the critical line σ = 1/2 is the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH)")

recognition.difference: The textbook statement is about primitive characters of modulus $q > 1$ and says that every non-trivial zero has real part $1/2$. The Lean statement says only that there is no zero with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$, and it includes modulus 1, that is $\zeta$. With the functional equation, which the Lean statement does not contain, the two agree for $q > 1$ (a zero to the left of the line gives one to the right for $\bar\chi$, page 333 again), and modulus 1 is the Riemann Hypothesis.
recognition.result: the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for the $L$-functions of primitive Dirichlet characters

conditions: The hypothesis has no exception at $s = 1$, also for the character of modulus 1 (whose $L$-function is $\zeta$): it holds there only because Lean gives $\zeta(1)$ the defined value $(\gamma - \log 4\pi)/2$, which is not $0$, where mathematics has a pole.
claim.text: If no $L$-function of a primitive character vanishes for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$, then $L(\chi, s) \ne 0$ for every Dirichlet character $\chi$ and every $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$, except a principal character at $s = 1$

citations.source: H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I (Cambridge University Press, 2006), Chapter 10
citations.where: Section 10.1, p. 334, equation (10.20) and the lines after it ("Thus $L(s, \chi)$ has all the zeros of $L(s, \chi^*)$", with further zeros only on the imaginary axis)

recognition.difference: The $L$-function of a Dirichlet character is the $L$-function of the primitive character that induces it, times a finite product of factors $1 - \chi^*(p)\,p^{-s}$ over the primes dividing the modulus; so the two have the same zeros off the imaginary axis. The book speaks of the zeros of the two functions. The library states non-vanishing: if no $L$-function of a primitive character vanishes for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$, then none of any character does, except that for the trivial character the point $s = 1$ is left out, where $\zeta$ has its pole. The hypothesis itself leaves no point out (see this step's condition). The product runs over the primes dividing the modulus, as in the book; the library takes it from Mathlib's lemma for a change of modulus.
recognition.result: the factorisation of a Dirichlet $L$-function through the primitive character that induces it

citations.where: Section 15.1, Lemma 15.1 (p. 463) and Theorem 15.2 with its proof (p. 464)

recognition.difference: In that form, a one-sided bound $x^\theta$ on an error term rules out zeros to the right of $\theta$. The book states this as an oscillation result for $\zeta$ alone: Theorem 15.2 says $\psi(x) - x = \Omega_\pm(x^{\Theta - \varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, where $\Theta$ is the supremum of the real parts of the zeros of $\zeta$, and the library's form is the contrapositive of its $\Omega_+$ half. The book assumes the bound for all large $x$ and takes the error term $\psi(x) - x$ of one function; the library assumes it only on windows $[Y, Y^{1+\delta}]$ for arbitrarily large $Y$, for a weighted sum over a family of characters of the smoothed sums $\sum \Lambda(n)\chi(n)(y/n - 1)$ with main terms removed. The textbook proof also expands at a fixed point, but it sums the whole Taylor series and rearranges it, which uses the sign for all large $x$; the library's proof uses one coefficient of high order at a time, whose weight lies in a single window up to a small tail. The book's proof of Lemma 15.1 is one sentence: the proof of Theorem 1.7 "can be adapted".
recognition.result: Landau's theorem on Dirichlet series with non-negative coefficients, in its error-term form

conditions: The theorem is stated for any type of families, any map from a family to its core data, and any one condition on a family at $x$. On the route of the release's main theorem these are the library's families, the map to their core data, and a condition on a family at $x$ (we have not opened its definition). The tied inequality with constants $c_D$ and $c_L$ says: for some further constants, the condition on the family holds at every large $x$ in the family's windows. Both conditions in the claim are defined through it. The window inequality says that for all $c_D$, $c_L$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, every family that satisfies a condition on the family at the level (we have not opened its definition) and the tied inequality with $c_D$, $c_L$ has $E_\Lambda(x) \le x^{1/2 + (c_D + c_L + 7)\varepsilon}$ at all large $x$ in its windows, where $E_\Lambda$ is the level's weighted error term. The statement that the level has families at scale $\lambda$ says that there are $c_D$, $c_L$ and $\varepsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_1$ some family satisfies the condition at the level, has windows at scale $\lambda$, and satisfies the tied inequality with $c_D$, $c_L$. The library's construction of the level from a subgroup, the condition on the family at the level, and the family's data are not opened.
claim.text: For a set $Q$ of primitive characters and one scale $\lambda > 1$: if, for each $\psi$ in $Q$, the level $\Lambda_\psi$ that the library builds from the powers of $\psi$'s character satisfies the window inequality and has families at scale $\lambda$, and has the Landau property, then $L(\psi, s) \ne 0$ for every $\psi$ in $Q$ and every $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$
